name: Brooks's Law
statement: Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.
meaning: Throwing more people at a project that is already behind usually pushes the finish line further out, not closer.
mechanism: New people are not instantly productive: someone already on the project has to stop working to train them, and every extra person multiplies the communication channels that must be kept in sync. For a while the ramp-up cost and the coordination overhead outweigh the added labour, so the schedule slips further before it improves — if it improves at all.

examples.text: Brooks's own arithmetic: n people have n(n−1)/2 pairwise links to keep in sync. Doubling a team from 5 to 10 people roughly doubles the headcount but takes the coordination paths from 10 to 45 — and a 50-person team carries 1,225 of them.

Brooks's analogy: 'While it takes one woman nine months to make one baby, nine women can't make a baby in one month.' Some work has sequential dependencies that no amount of added labour can compress.

A release is a month late, so five engineers are added in week one. The existing team spends the next fortnight explaining the architecture and untangling ownership; short-term output falls before the newcomers become net contributors, and the date slips again.

whyItMatters: It punctures the intuition that people and time are interchangeable — that a job needing twelve person-months can be done by twelve people in one. A late project is more often rescued by cutting scope or holding the team steady than by staffing up in a panic.

working.lead: Don't staff up a late project in a panic
working.text: the ramp-up and coordination costs land exactly when there is no slack to absorb them; adding people mid-crunch usually buys delay.

working.lead: Cut scope or hold steady instead
working.text: a late project is more often saved by shipping less, or by protecting the team it has, than by growing headcount.

working.lead: If you must add, add early and to separable work
working.text: new hands help before the crunch, and on partitionable tasks — testing, tooling, documentation — that need little coordination.
clean interfaces are what let more people work without more communication; the coordination cost the law punishes is a function of coupling.

limits: Brooks himself called the law an 'outrageous oversimplification', and it is deliberately narrow. Adding people early, before a project is late, can genuinely help; a project may be labelled 'late' only because its original schedule was fantasy; and adding highly skilled developers who already know the codebase avoids most of the ramp-up penalty. The law bites hardest on tightly-coupled, non-partitionable work under communication load — for genuinely divisible tasks, more hands really do produce more output. Strong modularity and clear ownership shrink the effect the law describes.
misreadings: It does not say adding people never helps — early, before the crunch, more hands can genuinely speed things up. The claim is narrow: adding people to an already-late project, mid-flight, tends to backfire because the onboarding and coordination costs land exactly when there is no slack to absorb them.
origin: Coined by the software engineer Fred Brooks in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month, drawing on his experience managing the development of IBM's OS/360. Brooks gave two mechanisms — the ramp-up time to train new people, and the communication overhead that grows as n(n−1)/2 — and freely described the law itself as an 'outrageous oversimplification' of a real tendency.

sources.text: Brooks, F. P. (1975; anniversary ed. 1995). The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering. Addison-Wesley.
